opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underrated levers. Right now the bottleneck for RL on white-collar work isn't really the algorithm. It's that you need a model with a good enough prior that it occasionally succeeds at the task. RL can only amplify behaviors the model already produces some fraction of the time. If the model has never seen how someone navigates a messy internal dashboard, reconciles a spreadsheet against an email thread, or bounces between Slack, Jira, and a codebase to close out a ticket, the success rate starts near zero and there's no signal to learn from.

Pre-training on large amounts of screen recordings would change that starting point. You'd get a model that has absorbed the texture of how work actually gets done: the sequences of clicks, the "check this other tab before you commit" habits, the recovery behaviors when something breaks. That's very hard to get from text on the internet, because people don't write down the tacit procedural stuff. Code was the exception, because programmers externalize their process into commits, Stack Overflow, and so on, and I think that's a big part of why coding has moved so fast.

So the RL tasks you can tackle become much longer-horizon and much more realistic. Instead of carefully scaffolded environments where you hand-build every tool, you can drop the model into something closer to a real computer, give it a goal like "prepare the quarterly report" or "onboard this vendor," and it has a reasonable shot at partial success. Then RL does what it's good at: sharpening, making it reliable, and teaching it to verify its own work.

The other piece is that screen recordings implicitly contain a lot of reward-relevant information. You see what the end state looks like when someone finishes the task, which gives you a way to construct verifiers or at least train reward models. That's been a huge constraint. Coding and math have nice verifiers. Most office work doesn't. Recordings let you get closer to "here's what done looks like."

There are real caveats. Privacy is a big one, and the data is enormously redundant. Most screen time is people scrolling or waiting, so you'd need to be smart about filtering and compression. And the observation is pixels, which is expensive compared to text tokens. But directionally, I think it shifts white-collar automation from "we need to build a bespoke environment for every job" to "we have a general computer-use prior, and RL just has to close the last mile." That's a much more scalable regime.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training gives the model a reasonable shot at longer, realistic tasks and that recordings show completed end states that can support verifiers or reward models.

r002.rationale: It connects screen-recording pre-training to achievable longer-horizon work trajectories, then explains that the recordings’ completed outcomes can enable outcome-based verification or reward models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people underrate about screen recordings is that they're not really a pre-training story, they're a prior story for RL. Right now, if you want to build an RL environment for, say, closing the books in some accounting software, you have to hand-build the environment, hand-specify the reward, and then the model has to stumble around until it figures out what a reasonable sequence of actions even looks like. The exploration problem is brutal, because the action space of a computer is enormous and almost every random click is useless.

If you've pre-trained on millions of hours of people actually doing the work, the model walks into that environment already knowing roughly what a competent person does. It knows that when the spreadsheet looks like this, you go to that menu. It's got the equivalent of having watched over someone's shoulder for a few years. So RL stops being about discovering the task from scratch and becomes about refining judgment at the margins, handling the weird cases, recovering from errors, chaining long sequences together without drifting. That's a much more tractable problem, and it means you can do RL on tasks that are way longer-horizon than you could otherwise.

The second thing it changes is what counts as a task. Today we're kind of constrained to things with verifiable rewards, code that compiles, tests that pass, math that checks out. A lot of white collar work isn't like that. It's "did this email handle the situation well," "did this slide actually make the point." Screen recordings give you an enormous amount of implicit supervision about what good looks like in those fuzzy domains, because you can see what people did, what got revised, what got sent back, what the downstream consequence was. You can train reward models off that. So the set of tasks you can do RL on expands from "things with a unit test" to "things a competent professional would recognize as done right."

And then the thing I'd flag is that it's also a demonstration of the mundane. Most of what happens on a screen in an office is tedious glue work, copying things between systems, reconciling, checking. That's exactly the stuff that's been hard to specify as a clean RL problem because no one would bother writing it down, but it's a huge fraction of the actual hours. Seeing it done at scale is what lets you target it.

The caveat is that you're learning from how humans use interfaces built for humans. In the long run I don't think the optimal agent clicks through menus. But as a bootstrap into a world where the model can then do its own RL and discover better strategies, I think it's probably one of the biggest unlocks there is, bigger than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response says screen-recording pretraining makes longer-horizon tasks more tractable and describes reward models for fuzzy outcomes, but it does not clearly say those tasks have easier-to-judge rewards conditional on reaching the rewarded outcomes.

r002.rationale: It explains that prior demonstrations make long action sequences achievable and that observed revisions, feedback, and downstream consequences can support reward models for outcome-focused tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think it would make the space of useful reinforcement learning tasks much broader. The hard thing about a lot of white collar work is that the task isn’t just, “Here’s a question; produce an answer.” It’s navigating a bunch of software, finding the relevant context, and figuring out what to do next.

If you’ve pretrained on people actually doing that work, then the model has some prior over what those trajectories look like. It’s seen someone go from a customer email to a spreadsheet, look something up in an internal tool, and then write a response. That doesn’t necessarily teach it to do the job reliably, but it gives reinforcement learning somewhere useful to start.

Imagine trying to train an agent to reconcile an invoice when it barely knows how to use the accounting software. Almost every rollout fails before it gets to the interesting part. If it already knows roughly how a person would approach the task, you can reward whether it actually reconciled the invoice correctly. You can train on longer tasks because success isn’t this vanishingly unlikely event.

The caveat is that recordings don’t automatically give you the reward signal. You see what someone clicked, but you may not know whether they made the right decision, or what information they had outside the screen. You still need environments where the agent can act and where you can judge the outcome. But demonstrations could move a lot of tasks from “we can’t get any traction with RL” to “we can now improve this through practice.”

r001.rationale: The response says longer tasks become trainable because successful rollouts are less unlikely and gives invoice correctness as a reward, but it does not state that the rewards are easier to judge.

r002.rationale: It explains that pretraining gives the agent a useful starting point, makes longer tasks achievable, and lets RL reward whether the task outcome—such as reconciling an invoice correctly—was achieved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would make a much broader set of tasks tractable. A lot of white-collar work happens through interfaces, and the final artifact doesn’t tell you how someone got there. You see the spreadsheet or the presentation, but you don’t see which documents they consulted, what they searched for, or how they checked their work. Screen recordings could give you some of that missing trajectory.

For reinforcement learning, that matters because the model needs to be able to do something useful before you can reliably reward it. If you put a model into a complicated enterprise application and it has no idea how to navigate it, getting a reward at the end of a two-hour task isn’t going to teach it very efficiently. If pre-training has already taught it the basic workflows, you can start training on whether it actually completes the task correctly.

The important caveat is that recordings don’t automatically give you a reward function. Watching someone update a financial model doesn’t tell you whether their assumptions were right. You still need tasks where you can check the outcome, or people who can judge it. But you could move from rewarding tiny, isolated actions to rewarding whole workflows, because the model would have a much better starting point.

r001.rationale: The response says models could be rewarded for completing whole workflows when outcomes can be checked, but does not state that long-horizon rewards can be easier to judge.

r002.rationale: It explains that pre-training teaches basic workflows, giving the model a better starting point for completing whole tasks and enabling training based on whether the outcome is correct.
